title: Community fills downtown Easton for Delmarva Pride Festival
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Community fills downtown Easton for Delmarva Pride Festival

 June 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 545
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hundreds walked up and down South Harrison Street Saturday for the Delmarva Pride Center's third annual Pride Festival, which featured vendors and booths from around the region.It was the third time back for some attendees, while others enjoyed a first-time experience. Ethan O'Donnell, a rising high school sophomore and resident of St. Michaels, was one of those first-timers.
"I really wasn't expecting to see this many queer people," O'Donnell said. "... I didn't realize there was actually this large community of people."
Kyle O'Donnell, the chair of the Delmarva Pride Center's board of directors, said the Easton location has been a good fit for the event, thanks to the business and people that are "already friendly to everyone."
"The response from the community and the residents and people all over Delmarva has just been wonderful," Kyle O'Donnell said. "99% of the people are coming at us with love, and positivity and kindness, and they recognize that we're their neighbor."
Some businesses and nonprofits set up booths with free giveaways, clothing and accessories for sale, and informational brochures. Deanna Zakes ran a tent for Free Mom Hugs, a national nonprofit that aims to celebrate the LGBTQ+ community.
Zakes is the organization's Eastern-Shore-area leader. She was adorned in rainbow attire and traversed the festival giving out hugs to attendees.
"It means acceptance, and love, and kindness and caring," Zakes said of the hugs. "Being wrapped in a hug by a mom … is one of the most healing things in the world. Every time I give a hug, I kind of feel like maybe I healed a little part of somebody who got broken somehow."
Originally from Baltimore, Zakes said she was at first unsure of the Eastern Shore's acceptance and tolerance toward the LGBTQ+ community.
"Being part of this has been really great because I'm finding like-minded people, and they're great," Zakes said.
"You just get to be reminded of how large of a community it is," attendee Ghost Carter said. "It's really nice to have that reminder."
FESTIVAL PERMIT
While the festival went on without a hitch Saturday, the public assembly permit for the event was passed by a narrow 3-2 vote in January at the hands of the Easton Town Council.
Council President Frank Gunsallus and Ward 3 council member David Montgomery were the two votes against the permit, with the latter expressing concerns of "overtly sexualized performances and behavior" at the festival in 2023.
During this year's event, Kyle O'Donnell said he was disappointed that there was not full support for the festival's permit from the council.
"I feel sad personally at where we are currently," O'Donnell said. "Because when we think back to our first year when we submitted the request to have a street festival, I didn't know what the response was gonna be from the town council. And it was unanimous and bipartisan. And so I feel that we've slid back a little bit.
"So if there is a request to make a change for Pride, that change needs to be for all the street festivals. We shouldn't be treating Pride Festival differently than anyone else."
O'Donnell said the center told musicians and performers to avoid curse words and keep it a "family-friendly event."
"We've got parents here with their kids," he said. "… This is representative of Easton, this is representative of Delmarva."

title: What's done in public matters
author: Staff Writer
content:
What's done in public matters

 June 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 360
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I have been following the debate on gay pride activities. Agreed: We should respect members of our community who identify as same-sex attracted or other forms of LGBTQ+ — and the Town Council must be fiscally responsible with the budget.Perhaps a four-day Pride festival brings in revenue. I don't have the facts on that, but I believe the festival politicizes a personal sexual preference.
Some of the events even seem designed to promote shock as well as pride. I understand that is a personal viewpoint, but it may be shared by others in the community. We live here together.
May I offer additional thoughts I have not seen addressed. As a mom, grandmother, teacher and active member of the community — I fail to see the wisdom in activities that sexualize or sensualize adults or children.
As a teacher I reminded students — and in a couple of cases adults — to show a little more modesty, and a little less PDA, high school "code" for "public display of affection."
Everything doesn't have to be public. We think it does, but it doesn't. Other recent Star Democrat articles have addressed internet activities that harm kids, teens (and adults).
We are working diligently as a society and a school system to teach kids that they are total human beings with brains, talents and abilities. They are not sexual objects. Online or in public.
Newspaper photos and events that entertain families sexually cannot in the long game be helpful. The human body is beautiful, but it is only one part of a person.
I think we as a society may be missing the big picture. Whether heterosexual, same-sex attracted, LGBTQ+ or any label we attach to our sexuality, our pride should never be in that.
Publicly flaunting a particular sexual preference seems to teach the next generation that their pride is in sex. That seems counterproductive to a healthy society and may do a disservice to all families and individuals.
Please consider my thoughts before you dismiss them. What we do in public matters. How we treat each other is a two-way street. I agree that this is not a game, so we need to respectfully talk this over.
HEATHER CROW
Easton

title: Juneteenth celebration brings people together, has them coming back for more
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Juneteenth celebration brings people together, has them coming back for more

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 391
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Academy Art Museum's Juneteenth celebration has fostered community in downtown Easton.People come back year after year, bringing family and friends with them, said Tyniece Savoy, who is the adult programs coordinator at the museum.
"A lot of folks of color did not feel welcome here," Savoy, who put the event together with the museum's Juneteenth Committee, said about the museum in the past. "They felt like maybe you had to have a membership or maybe it was just for certain activities. ... And now this is our 13th year throwing this celebration, so everyone's feeling more comfortable with this space."
That comfort was apparent Saturday afternoon — even in the sweltering heat — as event-goers danced, listened to live music, ordered from food trucks and drank lots of water. Anna Wilson, who has been attending the museum's Juneteenth celebration for more than a decade, said she couldn't complain about anything but the heat.
"It's hot, but it was wonderful," she said. "Everything was excellent."
Savoy said the museum was giving out free water and welcoming attendees inside the museum to cool off.
Throughout the afternoon, there was plenty of entertainment, from musical performances by Ayla Dennis, Ruby Fisher and Mid Shore Voices United to a fashion show featuring Black Squirrel Company, Buzz-Arts, NOT A PHASE Clothing and Dinah Wilson. Howard Barnett Jr., also known as DJ E-Shore, provided music for the event, and Devon Beck emceed it.
Beck, who is on the Juneteenth Committee, said the celebration had "family reunion vibes." He said that even in the heat, people stuck around.
Wilson, who said this celebration brings togetherness, said it's important that Juneteenth is celebrated.
"Because we need to know our history," she said.
Juneteenth, which became a federal holiday in 2021, marks the emancipation of enslaved African Americans.
Savoy's favorite part of the day was the fashion show. She said she was nervous because there was no dress rehearsal beforehand.
"But they brought so much energy," she said. "I mean it was just awesome."
Bringing the community together is part of the museum's mission, and holding events like this does just that, Savoy said. Over the years, she has noticed familiar faces from the museum's events come into the museum at other times throughout the year.
"They feel welcome," she said. "And now that the admission is free, it breaks all barriers. No one has to feel left out."

title: Delmarva Pride Center keeps Pride going year-round
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Delmarva Pride Center keeps Pride going year-round

 June 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 482
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Pride month celebrations are drawing to a close on the Eastern Shore, but for advocates of Delmarva's LGBTQ+ community, Pride was never about a single month, but maintaining community throughout the year.Kyle O'Donnell, chair of the Delmarva Pride Center, said the center was founded three years ago and hosts events year-round. It also has drop-in hours on Tuesdays and Saturdays.
"We have all types of activities from socials to support groups to game nights," O'Donnell said. "And we just want to have positive, family-friendly activities for people to come out and meet other queer people in the community and know that there is a home for them on Delmarva."
Events for the center include arts and crafts evenings, parents and allies groups on Saturdays, tabletop games, monthly social events at different locations, movie days, weekend coffee chats, and Dungeons and Dragons nights.
O'Donnell said the Dungeons and Dragons game nights were a great example of listening to community members. The game was a great way for people to engage in good fellowship together, to engage imagination and creativity and to think of who their ideal hero or champion would look like.
For members of Delmarva Pride Center like Rebecca Hutchinson, the center has given her a community of people who know what it's like to be LGBTQ+ while living in a conservative community.
"I can go to their events and know that I am safe, and I can be myself," Hutchinson said. "I know that I have emotional support if needed."
Hutchinson said she grew up on the Eastern Shore and now works as a mental health clinician. She has informed her clients, who are LGBTQ+ and seeking community, about the events and support groups that Delmarva Pride has.
This includes a Gender Expression Movement meeting every month hosted at the Unitarian Universalist Fellowship in Easton. This support group is for those who are exploring or identifying anywhere along the gender spectrum.
O'Donnell said the Elder and Intergenerational Social has been included on their calendar, an event to gather LGBTQ+ members from all generations to share their stories, experiences and wisdom.
According to O'Donnell, this event allows people to talk and learn how society has grown over time and what still needs to be resolved.
Hutchinson said that throughout her life as a member of the LGBTQ+ community, it has meant so much to her to have a center that provides the kind of support she sought as a native of the area.
"I grew up here, and I know what it was like to not see anyone that I thought was like me," Hutchinson said. "I didn't have any person or place to help me understand what I was struggling to figure out."
"Because of the Pride centers, there is representation, visibility, fun events and support available to anyone trying to figure out who they are or wanting to be around people who understand some of their experiences," she said.

title: Opinions are not persecution
author: Staff Writer
content:
Opinions are not persecution

 June 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 394
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On June 16, in an op-ed in The Star Democrat, Mr. Rudy Reyes accused the Republican Party of causing "fear of persecution" in the LGBTQ community, particularly in connection with a meeting of the Easton Town Council on June 3. While registered Republicans and members of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee may have attended that meeting, they attended as concerned citizens on their own behalf, not as representatives of the GOP.As for the council members themselves, Mr. Frank Gunsallus is not a Republican. Mr. David Montgomery is, but like the other Town Council members, he spoke on his own behalf, not on behalf of the Republican party. While individual members, myself included, may agree with Mr. Montgomery, he was not in that instance representing the GOP.
To be clear, the Republican Party, the party of Lincoln, does not endorse "persecution" of anyone. At any rate, after reviewing the video of the meeting, I fail to see how the words of either Mr. Gunsallus or Mr. Montgomery rose to the level of "persecution." If someone does not choose to celebrate or promote the LGBTQ agenda, it does not signify persecution. It may mean, however, that many people have come to view the Pride movement as a political movement which heavily identifies with the far left of the Democrat party.
That is where the words "socialism" and "ideology" come in. And we Republicans are as free to disagree with you Democrats about your ideologies as you are free to disagree with us. For instance, a Democrat might disagree with me about the human rights of an unborn child, but that does not mean I am being persecuted.
As for traditional holidays being about "feelings" let us be clear that Christmas is about the birthday of Jesus Christ, not feelings. St. Patrick's Day is about a man who preached the Gospel of Jesus Christ under brutal circumstances. On July 4, 1776, our founders were putting their lives in danger for their country. Most of our holidays are about sacrifice for the sake of God or country. Not feelings.
What I am wondering about is how drag queens came to epitomize the LGBTQ movement. I noticed on the Delmarva Pride Festival schedule that five drag queens are named as hosts. To many people drag is seen as mockery of women and degrading to femininity. Maybe women should feel persecuted.
MARY-EILEEN RUSSELL
Claiborne
